project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin is currently routed to internal fuel, so using it for another purpose would require changing that use.
There is no lignin dryer; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying equipment or an external drying step.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical modification equipment are not available at the mill.
The stream leaves as wet cake, and uncertain moisture affects dry tonnage and shipped mass.
Covered cake storage is limited, which constrains how much wet material can be held before dispatch or processing.
data_quality_notes: This is fictional demonstration data, not measured data from a real mill; all values are illustrative assumptions and must be replaced with mill production records and lab results before decisions.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are unreported.
The lignin measurement method is stated for illustration only, and moisture is identified as uncertain.
Annual volume and quality ranges are assumptions about variability, not measured operating ranges.
agent.summary: The fictional record describes washed softwood kraft lignin filter cake with a validated dry-matter balance and no reported failed checks. The recorded composition total check passes; three composition fields are missing. Treat all quantities and quality data as illustrative rather than evidence about a real mill.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-03#1: A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin for plywood and other wood-based panel adhesives; cited studies commonly describe replacement up to 50%, while UPM reports up to 80% for its lignin.
LPF resin is reported by UPM as industrially proven for veneer plywood and meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3; a laboratory study also tested resin in poplar plywood.

target_customers.statement: Plywood manufacturers and producers of other wood-based panels are the clearest implied customer types for LPF adhesive.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in conventional phenol-formaldehyde resin is the incumbent material lignin would partly replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before PF-resin use.
The cited UPM veneer-plywood resin is reported to meet EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3; UPM also reports formaldehyde-emissions measurements using EN 717-2.
A laboratory study reports that its resin formulation met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

limitations: The review’s typical replacement level summarizes published studies, not a single commercial plant, and its reported depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is not a delivered-feedstock specification.
UPM’s performance and cost claims are vendor claims without a cited test report; the lignin is BioPiva and its kraft status and composition are not stated.
The laboratory adhesive study used poplar plywood.
The reported global resin production figure is an undated forecast, and the cited market value is from 2019.
missing_information: No named buyers, documented sales volumes, current lignin purchase prices, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided.
The evidence does not establish whether Pinecrest’s wet cake can meet process or resin specifications; the feedstock profile also lacks molecular-weight and phenolic-hydroxyl measurements.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes a vendor claim of industrially proven LPF resin that meets a plywood bonding class, plus a review reporting TRL 9 for LignoBoost extraction combined with resin substitution. It does not document commercial sales to buyers, so it does not support score 4.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin has been studied as a partial polyol replacement in rigid PUR/PIR insulation foam and flexible polyurethane foam; evidence also covers polyurethane panels, coatings, and rubber replacement at the pathway level.
For flexible foam, authors suggest kraft-lignin formulations may suit heavy-duty foam, while organosolv lignin was the better fit for automotive flexible foam in the cited study.

target_customers.statement: Foam producers serving rigid insulation applications are an implied customer type, and the flexible-foam research identifies automotive and heavy-duty foam uses.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material being partly replaced in the cited polyurethane studies.

qualification_requirements.statement: In one rigid-foam study, 16 of 19 lignins at 30 wt% replacement passed measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications; two of the three failures used kraft lignin and failed compressive-strength and/or closed-cell-content requirements.
The study cites total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g as an acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam; this is total OH, not phenolic OH.
Kraft lignin requires significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach polyurethane target properties.
The flexible-foam study reports compression set below the standard’s limit of 60%, but does not name that standard in the evidence summary.

limitations: The rigid-foam results are laboratory cup tests across several lignin types, and the study does not report a kraft-only pass rate.
The 2013 rigid-foam study is laboratory-scale, examines high-density foam, and reports strength reductions; organosolv lignin performed better than kraft lignin.
Flexible-foam findings are laboratory results compared with automotive OEM requirements; odor was not measured in the study.
The reported TRL applies to a broad polyurethane category rather than specifically to kraft-lignin foam. The market figures are historical, with a 2023 forecast.
A review on commercialization was available only as an abstract.
missing_information: No named polyurethane buyers, commercial lignin-foam sales, purchase volumes, current lignin prices, or regional demand estimates are provided.
The evidence does not establish Pinecrest cake’s suitability; the profile lacks molecular-weight, phenolic-OH, and sodium measurements, and no total-OH result is provided.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents research studies and a review of lignin-based polyurethane uses, but does not document industry pilots, development partnerships, or commercial sales for the pathway. The broad market figures do not establish demand for Pinecrest lignin.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a carbon-fiber precursor, including for lightweighting applications; the evidence also covers hard carbon for sodium-ion and lithium-ion battery anodes and lignin-derived activated carbon.
The hard-carbon review reports comparisons for sodium-ion batteries, while the cited company material describes lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries.

target_customers.statement: Battery manufacturers and carmakers are explicitly identified in connection with qualification of lignin-based anode material; automotive lightweighting is an implied end-use market for carbon fiber.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is the named comparator for lignin-based carbon fiber.
Anthracite is compared with lignin as a hard-carbon feedstock for sodium-ion batteries.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The cited carbon-fiber work says the kraft lignin it examined needed purification before use, and softwood lignin needed a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning.
The company material states qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years; it does not provide specific battery-anode quality specifications.
The activated-carbon study reports no strict precursor-quality limits, while noting that lower precursor ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

limitations: Carbon-fiber precursor specifications are the most demanding carbon-material requirements and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; they are cited secondhand, and the study’s lignin was not from standard kraft pulping.
The 2009 carbon-fiber report found lignin-fiber mechanical properties at about 50% of the target; its cost figures are targets or estimates, not measured sales economics.
The GreenLight results are a project’s own summary, with modeled costs, and TRL 5 applies to precursor spinning rather than the complete chain.
The hard-carbon findings are review summaries of other studies; the cost basis is unspecified.
The activated-carbon study is laboratory-scale and uses zinc chloride activation.
The battery-anode pilot announcement and qualification information are company statements from 2021, and later status was not verified.
missing_information: No named buyers, current sales volumes, purchase prices, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided for the three carbon-material applications.

The evidence gives no Pinecrest-specific results for ash, volatiles, particulates, carbohydrate content, melt-spinnability, or battery-anode performance; the feedstock profile also lacks sodium content.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents a lignin-carbon-fiber project reaching TRL 5 for precursor-fiber production and a company-announced anode-material pilot line with buyer qualification activity. It does not document commercial sales to established buyers, so the evidence supports development activity rather than score 4.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin.
The mill would need a drying solution for buyers or processes requiring dry powder, and would need to address the current internal-fuel use and limited covered cake storage.

technical_maturity.statement: Evidence reports TRL 8 for producing biobased phenolic resins and TRL 9 for LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins; these are distinct technology scopes, and both map to technical-readiness score 5.

adoption_barriers.statement: A product would need qualification for panel-adhesive performance; cited UPM veneer-plywood resin met EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and reports formaldehyde-emissions measurement using EN 717-2.
There are no named buyers, documented sales volumes, purchase prices, contract terms, or regional demand estimates in the supplied market findings.
Pinecrest-specific suitability remains unestablished, including the missing molecular-weight and phenolic-hydroxyl measurements.

report.summary: Carbon materials is the only pathway ranked by the scoring engine, at rank 1, but its low feedstock-compatibility score and unassessed economics warrant validation before prioritization. Phenolic resins has a higher unranked attractiveness estimate, but remains insufficient data because feedstock compatibility and economics are unassessed. Polyurethanes is also insufficient data and has weaker current market and commercialization evidence. Prioritize feedstock tests, economics inputs, and buyer/partner validation to determine whether the provisional ordering should change.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
